---
title: Databases
icon: Database
description: Create databases, define typed tables, write rows, and query them with a fluent builder, all backed by real PostgreSQL with permissions enforced in the database.
---

import { ShieldCheck, KeyRound, Radio, FolderClosed } from 'lucide-react';

An Applad database is real PostgreSQL. You define **tables** with typed
**columns**, write **rows**, and read them back through a fluent query builder or
the REST API. Access is governed by [permissions](/build/permissions) that Applad
enforces with PostgreSQL row-level security, so a rule you set is a rule the
database keeps, not one your client is trusted to honour.

The shape is: a **database** holds **tables**, a table has **columns** and
**rows**. You define the schema once (from the console, a migration, or a setup
script), then your app reads and writes rows.

![The console Databases tab listing a project's databases](/screens/databases.png)
_Databases, tables, columns and rows are all browsable in the console, backed by real PostgreSQL._

<Callout title="Two kinds of caller">
  Defining databases, tables, columns and indexes is an operator task. Do it with
  a **server API key** (`x-applad-key`) from a trusted environment, not from
  end-user code. Reading and writing rows is what your app does at runtime, with
  the signed-in user's **session** (`Authorization: Bearer <secret>`). Both hit
  the same `/v1/databases` routes.
</Callout>

## The client

Client examples below use a project-scoped SDK client. See
[authentication](/build/authentication) for how a user signs in and how the session
token is attached.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
import { Applad } from 'applad';

const client = new Applad({ endpoint: 'https://api.applad.io', projectId: '<projectId>' });
const db = client.databases;
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final client = Applad(endpoint: 'https://api.applad.io', projectId: '<projectId>');
final db = client.databases;
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Build a database

Defining the schema and writing the first rows follows one path: create a
database, add a table, give it typed columns, refine it with indexes and
relationships, then write rows.

<Steps>

<Step>

### Databases

A database is a namespace for tables. Create one, and pass its id to everything
below.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const database = await db.createDatabase('app', 'app');
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final database = await db.createDatabase(name: 'app', databaseId: 'app');
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

`databaseId` is optional. Omit it and Applad generates one (the SDKs send
`unique()`). The full set of database operations:

| SDK (Dart) | SDK (JS) | Route |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `createDatabase(name:, databaseId:)` | `createDatabase(name, databaseId?)` | `POST /v1/databases` |
| `listDatabases()` | `listDatabases()` | `GET /v1/databases` |
| `getDatabase(id)` | `getDatabase(id)` | `GET /v1/databases/{id}` |
| `updateDatabase(id, name)` | `updateDatabase(id, name)` | `PUT /v1/databases/{id}` |
| `deleteDatabase(id)` | `deleteDatabase(id)` | `DELETE /v1/databases/{id}` |

`listDatabases()` returns `{ "total": <n>, "databases": [...] }`.

</Step>

<Step>

### Tables

A table is a typed collection of rows. Create it with the permissions that decide
who may read and write it:

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
await db.createTable('app', 'messages', {
  tableId: 'messages',
  permissions: ['read("users")', 'create("users")'],
  documentSecurity: true,
});
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
await db.createTable(
  databaseId: 'app',
  name: 'messages',
  tableId: 'messages',
  permissions: ['read("users")', 'create("users")'], // any signed-in user
  documentSecurity: true,   // each row may also carry its own permissions
);
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

`permissions` are `action("role")` strings applied to every row in the table.
`documentSecurity` turns on per-row permissions in addition to the table ones.
Both are covered under [Permissions](#permissions) below and in full on the
[permissions](/build/permissions) page. Omit `tableId` to have one generated.

| Operation | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Create table | `POST /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables` |
| List tables | `GET /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables` |
| Get table | `GET /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables/{tableId}` |
| Update table (`name`, `permissions`, `enabled`) | `PUT /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables/{tableId}` |
| Delete table | `DELETE /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables/{tableId}` |

</Step>

<Step>

### Columns

Columns are typed and added one at a time, each with its own type-specific
options. Every column type accepts `required` (reject rows that omit it),
`array` (store a list of that type), and `default`.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
await db.createStringColumn('app', 'messages', 'body', { required: true, size: 8000 });
await db.createIntegerColumn('app', 'messages', 'priority', { min: 0, max: 5, defaultValue: 0 });
await db.createBooleanColumn('app', 'messages', 'pinned', { defaultValue: false });
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
// A required string, capped at 8000 characters.
await db.createStringColumn(
  databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages',
  key: 'body', required_: true, size: 8000,
);

// An integer with a range.
await db.createIntegerColumn(
  databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages',
  key: 'priority', min: 0, max: 5, defaultValue: 0,
);

// A boolean with a default.
await db.createBooleanColumn(
  databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages',
  key: 'pinned', defaultValue: false,
);

// An enum constrained to a fixed set.
await db.createEnumColumn(
  databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages',
  key: 'status', elements: ['sent', 'delivered', 'read'], required_: true,
);
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Type-specific options:

| Type | Route suffix | Options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| String | `/columns/string` | `size` |
| Integer | `/columns/integer` | `min`, `max` |
| Float | `/columns/float` | `min`, `max` |
| Boolean | `/columns/boolean` | None |
| Enum | `/columns/enum` | `elements` (required) |
| Email | `/columns/email` | None |
| URL | `/columns/url` | None |
| Datetime | `/columns/datetime` | None |
| Rich text | `/columns/richtext` | None (editorial, see [Content mode](#editorial-content-mode)) |
| Media | `/columns/media` | None (editorial) |
| Point | `/columns/point` | None (editorial, a geographic point) |

<Callout title="Not every type has a typed SDK helper">
  The Dart client ships helpers for string, integer, boolean and enum columns;
  the JS client ships string, integer and boolean. The other types (float, email,
  url, datetime, and enum from JS) are created by calling the route directly, for
  example `POST /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables/{tableId}/columns/email` with a
  JSON body `{ "key": "contact", "required": true }`.
</Callout>

List and delete columns:

```dart
await db.listColumns('app', 'messages');
await db.deleteColumn('app', 'messages', 'priority');
```

`listColumns` returns `{ "total": <n>, "columns": [...] }`.

#### Validation rules

Beyond the type, a column can carry a `validation` object that the server checks
on every write and rejects with a field-named error. The rules are applied by
`validateRowData` in `databases/service.go`:

| Rule | Applies to | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `minLength` / `maxLength` | string values | length bounds, in characters |
| `pattern` | string values | a regular expression the value must match |
| `min` / `max` | numeric values | inclusive value bounds |
| `message` | any | a custom error message returned on any violation |

Pass it in the column body, for example creating a slug column that must be
lowercase and hyphenated:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/databases/app/tables/messages/columns/string \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "key": "slug",
    "required": true,
    "validation": { "pattern": "^[a-z0-9-]+$", "maxLength": 60, "message": "slug must be lowercase, digits and hyphens" }
  }'
```

<Callout title="Type helpers do not carry min/max; validation does">
  The `min`/`max` you pass to `createIntegerColumn` set the column's stored
  bounds metadata. The enforced numeric range on writes comes from the
  `validation` object above. Set both if you want the range both advertised and
  rejected on write.
</Callout>

#### Column-level permissions

A single column can be marked readable or writable independently of the row. Set
its permission list to some combination of `read` and `write`; a column the
caller cannot read is stripped from returned rows, and one it cannot write is
dropped from an update.

| Operation | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Get column permissions | `GET /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables/{tableId}/columns/{key}/permissions` |
| Set column permissions | `POST .../columns/{key}/permissions` with `{ "permissions": ["read"] }` |

The set call rejects anything other than `read` or `write` with a `400`
(`databases/handler.go` `setColumnPermissions`).

</Step>

<Step>

### Indexes

Add an index to speed up filters and ordering on a column. Give it a key, a type
(`key`, `unique`, or `fulltext`), and the columns it covers:

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
await db.createIndex('app', 'messages', 'by_created', 'key', ['created_at'], ['DESC']);
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
await db.createIndex(
  databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages',
  key: 'by_created', type: 'key',
  columns: ['created_at'], orders: ['DESC'],
);
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

`orders` is optional and pairs positionally with `columns`. List with
`listIndexes('app', 'messages')`, remove with `deleteIndex('app', 'messages', 'by_created')`.

</Step>

<Step>

### Relationships

A relationship is a typed link between two tables. Create it as a column on the
source table, naming the related table and the relationship type:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/databases/app/tables/messages/columns/relationship \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "relatedTableId": "users",
    "type": "manyToOne",
    "key": "author",
    "twoWay": false,
    "onDelete": "setNull"
  }'
```

`type` is one of `oneToOne`, `oneToMany`, `manyToOne`, `manyToMany` (defaults to
`oneToMany`). `twoWay` and `twoWayKey` create the reverse link on the related
table. The relationship is a real PostgreSQL foreign key, and `onDelete` maps
straight to its referential action (`databases/service.go` `CreateRelationship`):

| `onDelete` | PostgreSQL action | Effect when the related row is deleted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `setNull` (default) | `SET NULL` | the link column is cleared |
| `cascade` | `CASCADE` | the owning row is deleted too |
| `restrict` | `RESTRICT` | the delete is refused while a row still links to it |

List with `GET /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables/{tableId}/relationships` and
delete with `DELETE .../relationships/{relationshipId}`.

<Callout title="Related-column selection is not wired up yet">
  You can define relationships and they exist as real foreign keys, but expanding
  a related column inside a row query (the `select('author(name)')` form) is not
  applied by the server today. Fetch the related row by its id in a second call.
</Callout>

</Step>

<Step>

### Rows

A row is one record. Create, read, update and delete them at runtime with the
signed-in user's session.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const row = await db.createRow('app', 'messages', { body: 'hello', status: 'sent' }, {
  permissions: ['read("users")'],
});
const rowId = row['$id'];

await db.getRow('app', 'messages', rowId);
await db.listRows('app', 'messages', { limit: 25, offset: 0 });
await db.updateRow('app', 'messages', rowId, { data: { status: 'read' } });
await db.deleteRow('app', 'messages', rowId);
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
// Create
final row = await db.createRow(
  databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages',
  data: {'body': 'hello', 'status': 'sent'},
  permissions: ['read("users")'],
);
final rowId = row['\$id'];

// Read one
final one = await db.getRow(databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages', rowId: rowId);

// List (offset pagination)
final page = await db.listRows(databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages', limit: 25, offset: 0);

// Update (partial, send only the fields that change)
await db.updateRow(
  databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages', rowId: rowId,
  data: {'status': 'read'},
);

// Delete
await db.deleteRow(databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages', rowId: rowId);
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

`rowId` is optional on create; omit it for a generated id. `updateRow` is a
`PATCH` and merges: fields you leave out keep their current value. `listRows`
returns `{ "total": <n>, "rows": [...] }`.

</Step>

</Steps>

### System fields on a row

Every row carries system fields alongside your own columns. Your columns sit at
the **top level** of the row object, merged with these:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `$id` | The row's id |
| `$tableId` | The table it belongs to |
| `$databaseId` | The database it belongs to |
| `$createdAt` | When it was created (RFC 3339) |
| `$updatedAt` | When it was last updated |
| `$permissions` | The row's own permission strings (present when document security is on) |

```json
{
  "$id": "a1b2c3",
  "$tableId": "messages",
  "$databaseId": "app",
  "$createdAt": "2026-01-04T10:00:00Z",
  "$updatedAt": "2026-01-04T10:00:00Z",
  "$permissions": ["read(\"users\")"],
  "body": "hello",
  "status": "sent"
}
```

```dart
print(row['\$id']);      // system field
print(row['body']);     // your column, top-level
```

## Querying

`from(databaseId, tableId)` starts a query. Filters, ordering and pagination
chain onto it, and `get()` runs it:

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const result = await db
  .from('app', 'messages')
  .equal('status', 'sent')
  .greaterThan('priority', 0)
  .orderDesc('created_at')
  .limit(50)
  .get();

console.log(result.total);
for (const row of result.rows) console.log(row['body']);
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final result = await db
    .from('app', 'messages')
    .equal('status', 'sent')
    .greaterThan('priority', 0)
    .orderDesc('created_at')
    .limit(50)
    .get();

print(result.total);          // total matching rows (before limit/offset)
for (final row in result.rows) {
  print(row['body']);
}
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Chained filters combine with **AND**. The builder returns `{ total, rows }`.

### Operators

Each of these is a method on the builder. `field` is a column name; string
matches (`contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`) are case-insensitive.

| Method | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `equal(field, value)` | `field` equals `value` |
| `notEqual(field, value)` | `field` does not equal `value` |
| `lessThan(field, value)` | `field` is less than `value` |
| `lessThanOrEqual(field, value)` | `field` is less than or equal to `value` |
| `greaterThan(field, value)` | `field` is greater than `value` |
| `greaterThanOrEqual(field, value)` | `field` is greater than or equal to `value` |
| `contains(field, value)` | `field` contains the substring `value` |
| `startsWith(field, value)` | `field` starts with `value` |
| `endsWith(field, value)` | `field` ends with `value` |
| `search(field, value)` | full-text search on `field` (PostgreSQL `tsvector`) |
| `between(field, min, max)` | `field` is between `min` and `max`, inclusive of both ends |
| `isNull(field)` | `field` is `NULL` |
| `isNotNull(field)` | `field` is not `NULL` |

`between` binds both bounds as parameters and compiles to SQL `field BETWEEN
$min AND $max`, so it works for numbers, dates and any other ordered column:

```dart
// Everything created in Q1, priced 10 to 100.
final q1 = await db
    .from('app', 'orders')
    .between('created_at', '2026-01-01', '2026-03-31')
    .between('price', 10, 100)
    .get();
```

```dart
// Everything unread that mentions "deploy", newest first.
final hits = await db
    .from('app', 'messages')
    .notEqual('status', 'read')
    .search('body', 'deploy')
    .orderDesc('created_at')
    .get();
```

### Ordering and pagination

`orderAsc(field)` / `orderDesc(field)` sort the result; without one, rows come
back newest-first (`created_at` descending). `limit(n)` caps the page (default
25) and `offset(n)` skips rows:

```dart
// Page 2 of 25.
final page2 = await db
    .from('app', 'messages')
    .orderDesc('created_at')
    .limit(25)
    .offset(25)
    .get();
```

`total` on the result is the full count of matching rows before `limit`/`offset`,
so you can compute how many pages remain.

#### Cursor pagination

`cursorAfter(rowId)` pages by keyset instead of offset: pass the `$id` of the
last row you saw and the next call returns the rows that come after it in the
current sort order. It stays correct and fast as rows are inserted or deleted
between pages, where a large `offset` can skip or repeat rows and forces the
database to count past everything it skips.

The server orders by your `orderAsc`/`orderDesc` column (or `created_at`
descending by default) and tie-breaks on `id` so the order is total, then
returns everything strictly after the cursor row. `cursorAfter` supersedes
`offset` when both are set.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const page1 = await db.from('app', 'messages').orderDesc('created_at').limit(25).get();
const last = page1.rows.at(-1)!['$id'] as string;

const page2 = await db
  .from('app', 'messages')
  .orderDesc('created_at')
  .limit(25)
  .cursorAfter(last)
  .get();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final page1 = await db.from('app', 'messages').orderDesc('created_at').limit(25).get();
final last = page1.rows.last['\$id'] as String;

final page2 = await db
    .from('app', 'messages')
    .orderDesc('created_at')
    .limit(25)
    .cursorAfter(last)
    .get();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

### Selecting columns

`select('col1, col2')` projects only the columns you name, cutting the payload
when a row is wide but you need a few fields. The system columns `id`,
`created_at`, `updated_at` (and `_permissions` on a document-security table) are
always returned so each row can still be assembled. Omit `select` to get the
whole row.

```dart
// Just the id and title for a list view.
final titles = await db
    .from('app', 'posts')
    .select('id, title')
    .orderDesc('created_at')
    .get();
```

<Callout title="Related-column expansion is not applied">
  A `select` that names a relationship, such as `select('title, author(name)')`,
  returns the plain columns (`title`) and drops the `author(name)` part rather
  than expanding the linked row. Related-column expansion is not wired up yet, so
  fetch the related row by its id in a second call. Every non-relation column
  projects as expected.
</Callout>

## Upsert a row

`PUT /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables/{tableId}/rows/{rowId}` writes a row by
id: if a row with that `$id` exists it is updated, otherwise it is created. It is
the create-or-replace counterpart to the merging `PATCH` update.

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.applad.io/v1/databases/app/tables/messages/rows/msg_1 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <sessionSecret>" \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "$id": "msg_1", "data": { "body": "hello", "status": "sent" } }'
```

An existing row returns `200`; a new one returns `201`.

## Bulk writes

Three routes act on many rows in one request. Each iterates server-side and
reports how many succeeded; rows that fail a permission or validation check are
skipped rather than aborting the batch (`databases/handler.go` `bulkCreateRows`,
`bulkUpdateRows`, `bulkDeleteRows`).

| Operation | Route | Body | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bulk create | `POST .../rows/bulk` | `{ "rows": [ {..}, {..} ] }` | `{ "created": <n>, "rows": [...] }` |
| Bulk update | `PATCH .../rows/bulk` | `{ "rows": [ { "$id": "..", "data": {..} } ] }` | `{ "updated": <n> }` |
| Bulk delete | `DELETE .../rows/bulk` | `{ "ids": ["..", ".."] }` | `{ "deleted": <n> }` |

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/databases/app/tables/messages/rows/bulk \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <sessionSecret>" \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "rows": [ { "body": "one" }, { "body": "two" } ] }'
```

<Callout title="Partial success is silent">
  Bulk operations report only a count. A create that fails validation and one
  that succeeds return `{ "created": 1, ... }` with no per-row error list, so
  reconcile the count against what you sent if every row must land.
</Callout>

## Adjust a number or list in place

Three convenience routes change one field of one row on the server, so a client
does not have to read the current value first:

| Operation | Route | Body | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Increment | `POST .../rows/{rowId}/increment` | `{ "field": "views", "delta": 1 }` | adds `delta` to the numeric field |
| Decrement | `POST .../rows/{rowId}/decrement` | `{ "field": "stock", "delta": 1 }` | subtracts `delta` |
| Append | `POST .../rows/{rowId}/append` | `{ "field": "tags", "value": "new" }` | pushes `value` onto an array field |

<Callout type="warn" title="Server-side, but not a database lock">
  These are implemented as read-then-write on the API (`databases/handler.go`
  `atomicNumericOp`, `atomicAppend`): the server reads the row, computes the new
  value, and writes it back. That is convenient but not a single locked
  statement, so two increments racing on the same field can still lose one. For
  a true counter under contention, use a [transaction](#transactions) or the
  [SQL endpoint](#run-sql-against-a-database) with `SET x = x + 1`.
</Callout>

## Transactions

`POST /v1/databases/{databaseId}/transactions` runs a list of operations inside a
single PostgreSQL transaction: they all commit or, on the first error, all roll
back. This is the way to make several row writes across tables land together.

Each operation names a `method`, a `tableId`, and the `rowId` and `data` it
needs:

| `method` | Acts as |
| --- | --- |
| `create` (or `POST`) | insert a row; omit `rowId` for a generated id |
| `update` (or `PATCH`) | update the row named by `rowId` |
| `delete` | delete the row named by `rowId` |

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/databases/app/transactions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <sessionSecret>" \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "operations": [
      { "method": "create", "tableId": "messages", "data": { "body": "hi" } },
      { "method": "update", "tableId": "counters", "rowId": "c1", "data": { "n": 42 } }
    ]
  }'
```

The response is `{ "total": <n>, "results": [...] }`, one result per operation
carrying its `method`, HTTP `status`, and resulting `body`. An empty
`operations` array is a `400`.

## Run SQL against a database

`POST /v1/databases/{databaseId}/sql` executes one SQL statement against the
project's schema. It is how the console's SQL editor works, and it is bound by
the same PostgreSQL row-level security as every other read and write.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/databases/app/sql \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <sessionSecret>" \
  -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "statement": "SELECT status, COUNT(*) FROM messages GROUP BY status" }'
```

The response reports `columns`, `rows`, `rowCount`, and `executionMs`. A
statement is read-only unless you pass `"writeAllowed": true`, and even then the
guard rails in `databases/service.go` `ExecuteSQL` hold:

- **Your roles, not more.** The statement runs under the caller's resolved roles
  in an RLS-scoped transaction. There is no `roles` field on the request. A
  client cannot name an "admin" role to slip a policy.
- **DDL is refused.** `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `GRANT`, `REVOKE`
  and friends return a `400`. Use the tables, columns and indexes routes to
  change schema.
- **`SET` / `RESET` is refused.** They could drop the role sandbox mid
  transaction.
- **One statement per request.** A second statement after a `;` is rejected, and
  leading comments cannot be used to hide a blocked keyword.

`SELECT`, `WITH`, `SHOW`, `EXPLAIN` and `VALUES` run as queries and return rows;
anything else runs as a write and returns an affected-row count (and needs
`writeAllowed`).

## Import a CSV

Two routes load rows from a CSV file. Send it as `multipart/form-data` with the
file under the `file` field; both accept up to 32 MB.

| Operation | Route | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preview | `POST .../tables/{tableId}/import/csv/preview` | parse and return the first rows and detected columns without writing |
| Import | `POST .../tables/{tableId}/import/csv` | insert every row; returns `{ "imported": <n>, "failed": <n>, "errors": [...] }` |

An optional `columnMapping` form field (a JSON object) renames CSV headers to
column keys.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.applad.io/v1/databases/app/tables/messages/import/csv \
  -H "x-applad-key: <apiKey>" -H "x-applad-project: <projectId>" \
  -F "file=@messages.csv" \
  -F 'columnMapping={"Body":"body","Status":"status"}'
```

## Editorial content mode

A table can be switched into **content mode**, which layers a drafting workflow
on top of the same rows API without changing your columns. Enabling it adds
system fields (`status`, `slug`, `locale`, `published_at`, `entry_group`) and
indexes them, so an entry can be a draft or published, localised, and versioned
(`databases/content.go`).

| Operation | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Enable | `POST /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables/{tableId}/content` |
| Disable | `DELETE .../tables/{tableId}/content` |
| Publish a row | `POST .../rows/{rowId}/publish` |
| Unpublish a row | `POST .../rows/{rowId}/unpublish` |
| List a row's versions | `GET .../rows/{rowId}/versions` |

Once on, `listRows` accepts editorial shorthands as query parameters:
`?status=published` and `?locale=en` filter to that slice. Every create and
update on a content-mode table also records a numbered snapshot in
`row_versions`, which `/versions` returns newest first (up to 50).

<Callout title="Disabling never deletes">
  Turning content mode off only clears the flag. The added columns, published
  state and version history stay in place, so you can toggle it back on without
  losing anything.
</Callout>

## Permissions

Access to every table and row is governed by [permissions](/build/permissions), which
Applad enforces with PostgreSQL row-level security. Because the rule lives in the
database, it holds for the query builder, the REST API and the realtime read path
alike. The [permissions](/build/permissions) page is the full reference; the essentials
for databases:

A permission is an `action("role")` string. Actions are `read`, `create`,
`update` and `delete`. Roles are resolved **server-side from the caller's own
identity and team memberships** on every request. A client never sends its own
roles.

| Role | Matches |
| --- | --- |
| `any` | everyone, signed in or not |
| `users` | any signed-in user |
| `user:<id>` | one specific user |
| `team:<id>` | every member of a team |
| `team:<id>/<role>` | members of a team who hold a role |

### Table permissions vs. document security

A permission set on the **table** applies to every row in it, which is right for
"any signed-in user may read this table". Turn on **document security**
(`documentSecurity: true` when you create the table) and each row *also* carries
its own `$permissions`: access is granted when the table grants it **or** the row
grants it. That is what lets one shared table hold data that different groups see
different slices of.

```dart
// Readable by the channel's team, editable and deletable only by its author.
await db.createRow(
  databaseId: 'app', tableId: 'messages',
  data: {'channel_id': channelId, 'body': 'hello'},
  permissions: [
    'read("team:$channelId")',
    'update("user:$myUserId")',
    'delete("user:$myUserId")',
  ],
);
```

With that in place a member of the channel's team sees the message, a non-member
sees nothing, and only the author can change or remove it.

A table's permissions can also be read and rewritten on their own, without
touching the rest of the table definition:

| Operation | Route |
| --- | --- |
| Get table permissions | `GET /v1/databases/{databaseId}/tables/{tableId}/permissions` |
| Set table permissions | `POST .../tables/{tableId}/permissions` with `{ "permissions": [ { "action": "read", "role": "users" } ] }` |

<Callout title="Fails closed">
  A row that does not grant a caller `read` is simply invisible to them. List
  queries skip it rather than erroring. If you build a document-security table and
  see no rows, check that each row grants `read` to a role the caller actually
  holds.
</Callout>

### Owner column

If a table has an owner column (a column named `owner_id` or `user_id` holding
the id of the user who owns each row), that user always has full access to their
own rows, without you setting per-row permissions for them.

## Errors

| Status | When |
| --- | --- |
| `400` | Missing required field on a create call, or an invalid request body |
| `403` | The caller lacks permission to create, read, update or delete (code `permission_denied`) |
| `404` | The database, table, column or row does not exist |

A row that fails a column's validation rule (a required field left out, an enum
value outside `elements`, a number outside `min`/`max`) returns a validation
error naming the offending field.
